definition: An enumeration: a type that groups a fixed set of related cases, such as north, south, east, west. Cases can carry associated values, and Swift enums are value types.
A blueprint of methods, properties and requirements that a type promises to provide. Classes, structs and enums adopt a protocol by conforming to it.
Adds new functionality (methods, computed properties, initializers, protocol conformance) to an existing type without modifying its original source code.
Code written with placeholder types, like <T>, so one function or type works with many types while staying type-safe. Array<Element> is a generic type.
A self-contained block of code that can be stored, passed around and executed later, capturing values from its surrounding context. It is written with braces: { parameters in body }.

The @escaping attribute marks a closure parameter that may be called after the function returns, for example a completion handler. Non-escaping closures (the default) must finish before the function ends.
A statement that checks a condition and requires an else branch that exits the current scope (return, throw, break). It is used for early exits and keeps unwrapped values available afterwards.
A block of code that runs just before the current scope exits, no matter how it exits. It is handy for cleanup such as closing files or releasing locks.
A parameter keyword that lets a function modify the caller's variable. The caller passes the variable with an ampersand (&).
Gives an existing type a new, often shorter or clearer name. It does not create a new type.
A lightweight group of values, possibly of different types, treated as one compound value, such as (404, "Not Found"). Elements can be named or accessed by index.
A shortcut for reading and writing elements of a collection or custom type using square brackets, like array[0] or dict["key"]. You define one with the subscript keyword.
Declaring a new variable with the same name as one in an outer scope, which hides the outer one inside the inner scope. A common example is if let name = name.
The region of code where a name (variable, constant, function) is visible and valid, usually delimited by curly braces. A value declared inside a scope is not available outside it.
Swift naming convention: variables, functions and properties use lowerCamelCase (userName), while types use UpperCamelCase (UserProfile).
The compiler's ability to deduce a value's type from its initial value, so you can write let age = 30 without declaring Int.
Swift checks types at compile time and prevents mixing incompatible types, such as adding a String to an Int, catching many bugs before the app runs.
A function that takes another function or closure as a parameter, or returns one. map, filter, reduce, sorted and forEach are common examples.
A higher-order function that transforms every element of a collection with a closure and returns a new array of the results.
A higher-order function that returns a new collection containing only the elements for which a closure returns true.
A higher-order function that combines all elements of a collection into a single value, starting from an initial value and applying a closure to each element.
A higher-order function like map that also discards nil results and unwraps the rest, useful for converting strings to numbers safely.
The Result<Success, Failure> enum represents either a success value or an error. It makes success and failure explicit and works well with completion handlers.
Marks a function that can fail by throwing an error. Callers must use try (inside do-catch, or try?/try!) when calling it.
Swift's error-handling statement: code that may throw runs in a do block, and each error is handled in a matching catch clause.
The Error protocol marks types that represent failures. Enums are commonly used to define custom errors that can be thrown.
A protocol for types whose values can be safely shared across concurrency domains (tasks, actors). It helps the compiler prevent data races.
An attribute that makes code run on the main thread's actor. UI updates must happen there; SwiftUI views and UIKit classes are generally main-actor isolated.
A unit of asynchronous work in Swift concurrency, created with Task { }. It runs async code, can be cancelled, and is the bridge from synchronous to async contexts.
A bug where multiple threads access the same memory at once and at least one writes, giving unpredictable results. Actors and Sendable help prevent it.
Apple's low-level concurrency system (GCD). It runs work on queues such as DispatchQueue.main and DispatchQueue.global, and is older than async/await.
A closure passed to a function and called when an asynchronous operation finishes, often receiving a result or error.
A type marked @propertyWrapper that adds reusable behavior to a property when you annotate it, such as @State, @Published or @AppStorage.
A modifier for stored properties whose initial value is computed only the first time it is accessed. A lazy property must be declared with var.
A property that does not store a value but calculates it each time through a getter (and optionally a setter). It is declared with var and braces.
A property that holds a value as part of an instance of a class or struct, declared with let or var.
Code attached to a stored property that runs when its value changes: willSet runs just before, didSet just after the change.
Keywords that limit where code can be used: open, public, internal (default), fileprivate and private, from widest to narrowest visibility.
An access level that restricts a declaration to the enclosing type or extension in the same file. It is used to hide implementation details.
A keyword for struct or enum methods that modify the instance's own properties. Without it, methods of value types cannot change self.
An initializer Swift automatically generates for structs, with one parameter per stored property, such as User(name: "Ana", age: 30).
A special method (init) that prepares a new instance by setting all its stored properties. Types can have several initializers.
A deinitializer called just before a class instance is deallocated. Use it to free resources; it only exists for classes.
A type whose instances are copied when assigned or passed around. Structs, enums, tuples and basic types like Int and String are value types.
A type whose instances are shared by reference: copies point to the same object. Classes, closures and actors are reference types.
A class can inherit properties and methods from a superclass and customize them with override. Structs and enums do not support inheritance.
The ability to treat different types through a common interface, such as a superclass or protocol, so each type responds in its own way.
Calling properties or methods on an optional with ?, such as user?.address?.city. If any link is nil, the whole expression is nil.
Safely unwrapping an optional with if let or guard let, which runs code only when the optional contains a value.
The ?? operator returns the optional's value if present, otherwise a default, as in name ?? "Guest".
Using ! to extract an optional's value, which crashes the app if it is nil. Prefer optional binding or ?? instead.
A control-flow statement that compares a value against patterns. It must be exhaustive and does not fall through, and works with enums, ranges and tuples.
An ordered collection of values of the same type, accessed by integer index starting at 0, such as [Int] or Array<String>.
An unordered collection of key-value pairs, written [Key: Value]. Looking up a key returns an optional.
An unordered collection of unique values of a Hashable type. It is fast for membership checks and supports union and intersection.
A sequence of values between two bounds: 1...5 is closed (includes 5) and 1..<5 is half-open (excludes 5).
Embedding values inside a string literal with \(value), such as "Hello, \(name)!".
A protocol that lets values be compared with == and !=. Swift can synthesize it automatically when all properties are Equatable.
A protocol for values that can produce a hash, required for Set elements and Dictionary keys. It builds on Equatable.
A protocol requiring a stable id property so SwiftUI (List, ForEach) can tell items apart.
A protocol that lets values be ordered with <, >, <= and >=, enabling sorting.
The opaque return type keyword, as in some View. It hides the exact concrete type while the compiler still knows it.
Keyword for existential types, as in any Shape: a box that can hold any value conforming to a protocol.
A symbol that performs an operation, such as +, ==, && or ??. Swift lets you overload operators or define custom ones.
Apple's built-in tool (SPM) for adding and managing dependencies. In Xcode, use File > Add Package Dependencies; a Package.swift file describes a package.
Apple's integrated development environment (IDE) for building apps for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, Apple TV and Apple Vision Pro. It includes the editor, compiler, Simulator and debugging tools.
An Xcode .xcworkspace file that groups one or more projects and their dependencies so they build together. CocoaPods creates one.
The left panel of Xcode with tabs such as Project, Source Control, Symbol, Find, Issue, Test, Debug and Report navigators.
The right panel of Xcode (utilities area) showing details and settings for the selected item, such as the Attributes, Size and Identity inspectors.
An Xcode scheme defines which targets to build, which build configuration to use, and what to run, test or profile. You choose it in the toolbar.
A set of instructions in an Xcode project to build one product, such as an app, a framework or a test bundle, with its own settings and files.
An Xcode tool that runs a virtual iPhone, iPad or other Apple device on your Mac for testing apps without real hardware.
A marker on a line of code that pauses execution so you can inspect variables and step through code. Click the line number gutter in Xcode to set one.
The debugger used by Xcode. In the debug console you can print values (po, p), evaluate expressions and control execution while paused.
An Xcode profiling app that measures performance, memory use, energy and more, with templates like Time Profiler, Leaks and Allocations.
An Xcode file (Assets.xcassets) that organizes images, app icons, colors and data sets, with variants for screen scales and Dark Mode.
The Info property list: a file describing app configuration such as display name, version and required permission descriptions (for example NSCameraUsageDescription).
An Interface Builder file (.storyboard) that visually lays out UIKit screens and the segues connecting them.
An Interface Builder file (.xib) that designs a single view or view controller interface, often for a reusable view or table cell.
A file listing special capabilities an app is allowed to use, such as iCloud, Push Notifications or App Groups. They are embedded when the app is signed.
A feature you enable in Xcode's Signing & Capabilities tab, such as Push Notifications, iCloud or HealthKit, which updates entitlements and the App ID.
A named set of build settings; new projects have Debug (for development and debugging) and Release (optimized for distribution).
The folder where Xcode stores build products, indexes and logs. Deleting it can fix strange build problems.
An Xcode document for experimenting with Swift code and seeing results immediately, without building a full app. Swift Playgrounds is also an app for iPad and Mac.
In SwiftUI, the View protocol describes a piece of UI through a body property. In UIKit, UIView is the base class for visible elements.
Apple's declarative framework for building user interfaces on all Apple platforms: you describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and it updates automatically.
The required computed property of a SwiftUI View that returns its content, of type some View.
A result builder (@ViewBuilder) that lets you list several views in a closure and combines them into one, as in the body of a VStack.
A method called on a SwiftUI view that returns a modified view, such as .padding(), .font() or .foregroundStyle(). Order matters.
A property wrapper for simple value state owned by a SwiftUI view. When it changes, SwiftUI re-renders the view's body.
A property wrapper that creates a two-way connection to state owned elsewhere. Pass one with a dollar sign, like $isOn.
A macro from the Observation framework (iOS 17+) that makes a class observable. SwiftUI updates only the views reading properties that changed.
A property wrapper that creates bindings to the properties of an @Observable object, for example to pass to a TextField.
A property wrapper that reads a value from SwiftUI's environment, such as colorScheme, dismiss or a shared model.
An older property wrapper that makes a SwiftUI view own an ObservableObject instance for the life of the view. @State with @Observable replaces it in new code.
A property wrapper inside an ObservableObject that announces changes to subscribers, so views using it refresh.
A property wrapper that reads and writes a value in UserDefaults and refreshes the view when it changes.
A principle where each piece of data has one owner and other views read or bind to it, avoiding conflicting copies.
A SwiftUI container that manages a stack of screens with push and pop navigation, used with NavigationLink or navigationDestination.
A SwiftUI control that navigates to another view when tapped, inside a NavigationStack.
A SwiftUI container that shows a tab bar to switch between top-level sections of an app.
A SwiftUI container that shows rows of data in a scrolling, single-column list, with support for sections, swipe actions and selection.
A SwiftUI view that creates views from a collection of data. Items need to be Identifiable or an id key path must be provided.
A SwiftUI container for grouping data-entry controls such as TextField, Toggle and Picker in a platform-appropriate style.
A SwiftUI container that arranges its child views vertically. Its siblings are HStack (horizontal) and ZStack (layered).
A SwiftUI container that layers its child views on top of each other, back to front.
A vertical stack that creates its child views only when they are about to appear on screen, which is efficient for long scrolling content.
A SwiftUI grid that lays out views in flexible columns and creates them lazily, configured with GridItem.
A SwiftUI container that lets its content scroll when it is larger than the available space.
A flexible SwiftUI view that expands to push other views apart along the stack's axis.
A SwiftUI container that gives its content the size and position of the available space through a GeometryProxy, for adaptive layouts.
A modal view presented over the current screen, in SwiftUI with the .sheet modifier. It is dismissed by swiping down or by code.
A small modal dialog that shows a message and buttons, in SwiftUI with the .alert modifier or in UIKit with UIAlertController.
A smooth transition between states. In SwiftUI you use withAnimation { } or the .animation modifier, with curves such as .easeInOut or .spring.
Xcode's canvas showing a live rendering of a SwiftUI view while you edit it, defined with the #Preview macro.
A SwiftUI modifier that runs a closure when a view appears on screen. .task is the async alternative.
Apple's imperative framework for building iOS and iPadOS interfaces with views and view controllers, still widely used and interoperable with SwiftUI.
An attribute (@IBOutlet) that connects a view in Interface Builder to a property in code so you can read or change it.
An attribute (@IBAction) that marks a method as callable from Interface Builder, for example when a button is tapped.
Xcode's visual editor for designing UIKit interfaces in storyboards and xib files by dragging objects and setting constraints.
A UIKit system that positions and sizes views using constraints that describe their relationships, so layouts adapt to screen sizes.
A rule in Auto Layout, such as 'leading edge equals 16 points from the superview', that determines a view's position or size.
A UIKit view that arranges its subviews in a row or column and manages their spacing and alignment automatically.
The UIKit class that manages a screen's view and its lifecycle, with methods like viewDidLoad and viewWillAppear.
A storyboard transition between two view controllers, such as show or present modally. You can prepare data in prepare(for:sender:).
A design pattern where one object hands off some responsibility or events to another through a protocol, as with UITableViewDelegate. Delegate properties are usually weak.
A UIKit protocol adopted by an object that supplies the data a view displays, such as UITableViewDataSource providing rows and cells.
A UIKit view that shows a scrolling single-column list of rows (cells), driven by a data source and delegate.
A UIKit view that displays items in flexible layouts such as grids, using cells and a layout object.
A string that lets a table or collection view recycle off-screen cells with dequeueReusableCell(withIdentifier:), saving memory.
The part of the screen not covered by the notch, Dynamic Island, home indicator or bars. Content should stay inside it unless it is a background.
The sequence of events a view controller goes through: viewDidLoad, viewWillAppear, viewDidAppear, viewWillDisappear and viewDidDisappear.
A trait (compact or regular) describing available width and height, used to adapt layouts across iPhone, iPad and orientations.
A simple key-value store for small user settings that persists between launches. It is not meant for large or sensitive data.
A typealias for Encodable and Decodable. Types conforming to it can be converted to and from formats like JSON using JSONEncoder and JSONDecoder.
JavaScript Object Notation: a lightweight text format for data made of objects, arrays, strings, numbers and booleans, widely used by web APIs.
Apple's framework (iOS 17+) for modeling and persisting data using Swift code and macros, built on Core Data technology and integrated with SwiftUI.
The SwiftData macro applied to a class to make it a persistent model whose properties are saved in the store.
A SwiftData property wrapper that fetches model objects and keeps a SwiftUI view updated, with optional sorting and filtering.
The SwiftData object used to insert, delete and save model objects. Views usually read it from the environment.
Apple's older persistence framework for object graphs, with a data model editor, managed objects and a managed object context. It can store data in SQLite.
Apple's framework for storing app data in iCloud and syncing it across a user's devices, using containers and databases.
Apple's encrypted secure storage for small secrets such as passwords and tokens, accessed through the Security framework.
Foundation's API for network requests such as downloading data or calling web services, with async methods like data(from:).
A web service style where resources are accessed through URLs and HTTP methods like GET, POST, PUT and DELETE, usually exchanging JSON.
The protocol of the web. Requests have a method, URL, headers and optional body; responses have a status code such as 200 (OK) or 404 (Not Found).
A Foundation class for working with files and folders in the app's sandbox, such as the Documents directory.
Security isolation that limits an app to its own container and approved resources, so apps cannot read each other's data.
Saving data so it survives after the app closes, using options such as UserDefaults, files, SwiftData, Core Data or iCloud.
Apple's framework for processing values over time with publishers and subscribers. It is used by @Published and ObservableObject.
An automated test that checks a small piece of code, such as a function, in isolation. Fast, repeatable tests catch regressions.
Apple's original testing framework. Test classes inherit from XCTestCase and assert with XCTAssertEqual, XCTAssertTrue and similar functions.
Apple's modern testing framework using the @Test attribute and #expect macro, with parameterized tests and a more readable syntax.
An automated test that launches the app and interacts with its interface by tapping and typing, using XCUIApplication.
A practice of writing a failing test first, then the code that makes it pass, then refactoring (red, green, refactor).
Restructuring code to improve readability or design without changing its behavior. Tests help ensure nothing breaks.
Finding and fixing bugs by reading logs, setting breakpoints, inspecting variables and reproducing the problem.
Apple's service for distributing beta builds to internal and external testers and collecting their feedback before App Store release.
Apple's web portal for managing apps: creating app records, uploading builds, TestFlight, metadata, pricing, reviews and sales reports.
A file linking an app ID, certificates and, for development, registered devices, which allows an app to run on devices or be distributed.
Cryptographically signing an app with a certificate so Apple and users can verify who made it and that it was not altered. Xcode can manage it automatically.
A digital credential issued by Apple that proves your identity as a developer and is used to sign apps, such as Apple Development or Apple Distribution.
A unique reverse-domain string, like com.company.MyApp, that identifies an app across Apple's systems.
Apple's process of checking submitted apps against the App Review Guidelines for safety, performance, business, design and legal rules before release.
A PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file declaring what data an app and its SDKs collect and which required-reason APIs they use.
ATT: a framework that requires apps to ask permission before tracking users across other companies' apps and websites. The prompt is shown with ATTrackingManager.
Apple's framework for in-app purchases and subscriptions, letting apps load products, handle purchases and check entitlements.
Content or features sold inside an app, such as consumables, non-consumables or subscriptions, handled through StoreKit.
A message sent to a device through Apple Push Notification service (APNs) even when the app is not running. It requires user permission.
The states an app moves through (not running, inactive, active, background, suspended). In SwiftUI, scenePhase reports them.
The Human Interface Guidelines: Apple's design recommendations for creating intuitive, consistent apps on each platform.
An iterative process: research, define, ideate, prototype, test and refine. Feedback from users guides each round.
An early, simplified version of an app used to explore ideas and test with users before full development.
A simple, low-detail sketch of a screen's layout showing where elements go, without colors or final visuals.
A short sentence describing a need from the user's view: 'As a [user], I want [goal] so that [benefit].'
UX: how a person feels when using a product, including usability, clarity and efficiency. User interface (UI) is the visual part of it.
Designing apps so people with disabilities can use them, with support for VoiceOver, Dynamic Type, sufficient contrast and Reduce Motion.
Apple's built-in screen reader that speaks what is on screen. Apps support it with accessibility labels, hints and traits.
A short text read by VoiceOver to describe an element, set with .accessibilityLabel in SwiftUI or accessibilityLabel in UIKit.
A system feature that lets users choose their preferred text size. Apps support it by using text styles such as .body and .headline.
A system-wide dark appearance. Apps adapt using semantic and asset catalog colors that change automatically.
Adapting an app to different languages and regions, with translated strings in String Catalogs and locale-aware dates, numbers and currencies.
Preparing an app so it can support many languages and regions, for example by avoiding hard-coded text and supporting right-to-left layouts.
Apple's library of thousands of scalable icons that match system text, used with Image(systemName:) in SwiftUI.
Tactile feedback through vibrations of the device's Taptic Engine, such as UIImpactFeedbackGenerator or SwiftUI's sensoryFeedback.
Apple's framework for running trained machine learning models on device, using the .mlmodel or .mlpackage format.
Apple's tool, as a Mac app (opened from Xcode) and as a framework, for training custom machine learning models such as image or text classifiers from your own data without much code.
Apple's framework for computer vision tasks such as text recognition, face detection, barcode reading and image classification.
Apple's framework for analyzing text: detecting language, tokenizing, tagging parts of speech and sentiment.
Apple's framework for using the on-device language model of Apple Intelligence in apps, for generating and structuring text privately.
A machine learning model that runs locally on the device rather than a server, giving better privacy, offline use and low latency.
A field of AI where computers learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions, instead of following hand-written rules.
The labeled examples used to teach a machine learning model. Its quality and diversity strongly affect accuracy and bias.
A distributed version control system that records changes as commits. Xcode has built-in Git support in the Source Control navigator.
A saved snapshot of changes in version control with a message that explains what and why.
An independent line of development in Git, used to work on a feature without affecting the main code until it is merged.
Application Programming Interface: the set of types, functions and rules a framework or service exposes so other code can use it.
A bundle of reusable code and resources, such as UIKit, SwiftUI or Foundation, imported with import. You can also build your own.
The base framework with essential types such as String, Date, URL, Data, JSONDecoder and UserDefaults.
The thread where the user interface runs. Long work there freezes the app, so heavy tasks go in the background and UI updates return to the main thread.
Memory that is never released because something still references it, often from a retain cycle. It makes the app grow in memory use.
A list in square brackets at the start of a closure, such as [weak self], that controls how values are captured and helps avoid retain cycles.
Model-View-Controller: a pattern separating data (model), interface (view) and the logic connecting them (controller). It is the traditional UIKit pattern.
A type with a single shared instance for the whole app, such as UserDefaults.standard. It is convenient but can make testing harder.
Passing the objects a type needs into it from outside instead of creating them inside, which makes code flexible and easier to test.
A secret string identifying your app to a web service. It should never be hard-coded in a public repository.
A SwiftUI view that downloads and shows an image from a URL, with placeholder and error phases.
Swift's built-in model for asynchronous and parallel code using async/await, Task, actors and structured concurrency.
